subject: Business Management
distinctive: Business management is in the individuals and societies group, so your essay explores a question about human experience and behaviour. The guide's business management examples each focus on one real organisation. One essay looks at how McDonald's trains its managers. The other looks at McDonald's relationship with its charity, Ronald McDonald House Charities. The guide's sport example also points to a case study: a brand sponsoring a football club.

Your content alone won't make your essay a business management essay. Business management concepts, methods and theories give you insight and help you build a well-constructed argument. The same broad interest, such as sport, could become a business management essay or a global politics essay. Your approach decides which.

The aims for the whole individuals and societies group apply to you too. Your essay lets you challenge assumptions about the social world and build your knowledge by reading the subject literature. You'll also select theories or concepts and apply suitable methods to build an argument.

sources.primary: Primary research is data you collect yourself, such as interviews and surveys. In the guide's Hamburger University example, the student interviews trainers and surveys graduates. Not every business management essay needs primary research: the guide's second example uses secondary data only.
sources.secondary: Every extended essay must include secondary research (a literature review). In the guide's first example, secondary sources describe and evaluate McDonald's training courses. In the second example, recent academic articles about Ronald McDonald House Charities supply the evidence.

methods: Case study of one organisation: the guide's sport example analyses a case study of a brand sponsoring a football club.
Describe and evaluate one practice of an organisation using secondary sources, supported by findings from your own primary research.
Primary research: interview people who carry out the practice and survey people who experienced the practice, as in the Hamburger University example.
Secondary data only: weigh up the advantages and disadvantages of a business relationship, as in the Ronald McDonald House Charities example.

Other research strategies for all individuals and societies subjects: comparisons, case studies, discourse analysis, critical analysis of a theory or concept, and in-depth analysis of a primary source.
choosing_topic: Your topic can come from your own life, from a current debate, from a topic in one of your favourite subjects, or from a topic related to a favourite subject but not covered in it.
Big real-world issues, such as the future of global capitalism, can work. Turn the issue into a focused question and explore it from a business management point of view.

Your topic must be considered in terms of one individuals and societies subject. A broad interest such as sport could fit several subjects. The guide's business management version analyses a brand sponsoring a football club.
Your approach decides your subject. The concepts, methods and theories of business management are what ground your topic in business management.

examples.topic: How McDonald’s trains its managers in the USA: The Hamburger University in Chicago
examples.rq: To what extent is McDonald’s Hamburger University an optimal form of training?
examples.why: The essay uses secondary sources to describe and evaluate McDonald's in-house training courses. Primary research supports the evaluation: interviews with trainers at Hamburger University and surveys of Hamburger University graduates.

examples.topic: McDonald’s charitable work: Ronald McDonald House Charities (RMHC)
examples.rq: Who benefits more from the relationship: RMHC or McDonald’s?
examples.why: Many recent academic articles discuss RMHC. Some praise the charity, and others criticise the charity because donations could be larger. Using secondary data only, the essay discusses the advantages and disadvantages of the relationship between McDonald's and RMHC.

structure: Make sure your research question and research methods clearly fit business management. The guide suggests reading the business management subject guide to check that you understand the subject and its methods.
Keep your argument within the logic of business management: use the subject's terms and follow its usual style and structure.
In the Hamburger University example, secondary sources carry the description and evaluation, and primary research findings support the evaluation.
Label diagrams, images and graphs clearly, acknowledge any made by others, and refer to each one directly in the body of your essay.
Use headings to organise your essay where they help.
pitfalls: Relying on content alone. Without business management concepts, methods and theories, your essay won't be grounded in business management.
A research question or research methods that don't clearly fit business management.
Writing without business management terms. The guide says that using the subject's terms shows you understand the subject.
A one-sided discussion. A balanced discussion looks at different perspectives on your topic, and your evaluation should weigh up the strengths and limitations of your essay.
Using sources or methods without checking that they suit business management. Ask your supervisor and read the business management subject guide.
Diagrams or graphs that are unlabelled, unacknowledged, or never referred to in the body of your essay.
rules: Your essay must include secondary research (a literature review).
Your topic must be considered in terms of business management, even if the same topic could be approached through another individuals and societies subject.
think: Which one real organisation is at the centre of your idea?
Which business management concepts or theories would you use to analyse the organisation's practice or decision?
Can secondary sources answer your research question, or do you need interviews or surveys with people inside the organisation?
Without business management concepts, would your question become an economics or global politics question?
Whose views would a balanced discussion of the organisation's practice need to include?

subject: Economics
distinctive: Economics is in the individuals and societies group, so your essay explores a question about human experience and behaviour. Both of the guide's economics examples set an economic theory or idea against evidence. One essay tests the neoclassical argument about minimum wages against current research. The other judges how far mobile banking has helped economic development in one town or village.

Your content alone won't make your essay an economics essay. Economics concepts, methods and theories give you insight and help you build a well-constructed argument. Use economics terms such as “supply and demand” to explain your analysis, and don't just drop them in as labels. Using terms that way shows you understand the subject.

Individuals and societies subjects can tackle big questions about our shared present, past and future. The guide names the future of global capitalism as one such issue. In an economics essay, you turn a big issue into a focused question and explore it from an economics point of view.

sources.primary: Primary research is data you collect yourself, such as surveys, interviews or local prices. In the guide's mobile banking example, primary research in one town or village shows how far economic development has happened there. Not every economics essay needs primary research: the guide's minimum wage example uses published research only.
sources.secondary: Every extended essay must include secondary research (a literature review). The minimum wage example researches the neoclassical argument and the studies behind the counterarguments. The mobile banking example includes data that other researchers obtained through randomised control trials.

methods: Test an economic theory against current research: present the theory, then research the counterarguments. Judge each counterargument by the nature of its evidence and the studies carried out.
Use recent evidence from news articles or data banks to test a link between two variables, such as minimum wages and unemployment, in different places.
Combine primary research in one place with data that other researchers obtained through randomised control trials. Then judge how far an outcome, such as economic development, has happened.

Other research strategies for all individuals and societies subjects: comparisons, case studies, discourse analysis, critical analysis of a theory or concept, and in-depth analysis of a primary source.
choosing_topic: Your topic can come from your own life, from a current debate, from a topic in one of your favourite subjects, or from a topic related to a favourite subject but not covered in it.

Big real-world issues, such as the future of global capitalism or the environmental and climate crisis, can work. Turn the issue into a focused question and explore it from an economics point of view.
Your topic must be considered in terms of one individuals and societies subject, even though many topics could fit more than one subject in the group.
Your approach decides your subject. The concepts, methods and theories of economics are what ground your topic in economics.
The guide's economics examples narrow their focus with a named theory (the neoclassical argument about minimum wages) or a named place and start date (town or village “X” since 2010).

examples.rq: Does current economic research into minimum wage invalidate the neoclassical argument that increasing the minimum wage will lead to increased levels of unemployment?
examples.why: Neoclassical economics argues that raising the minimum wage raises unemployment. Newer research argues that the neoclassical argument rests on flawed assumptions. The essay presents the neoclassical argument, then judges each counterargument by the nature of its evidence and studies. Recent evidence from news articles or data banks can test the link between minimum wages and unemployment in different places. Each point of analysis ends with a conclusion, and those conclusions build towards a judgement on how valid the neoclassical model is.

examples.topic: The role of mobile banking in economic development
examples.rq: How has increased access to mobile banking contributed to economic development in town (or village) “X” since 2010?
examples.why: The essay first researches how mobile banking can help economic development in theory, including data that other researchers obtained through randomised control trials. The essay looks at areas of development such as higher incomes, health and education outcomes, the empowerment of women and civic participation. Primary research then leads to a judgement of how far economic development has happened in the area studied.

structure: Make sure your research question and research methods clearly fit economics. The guide suggests reading the economics subject guide to check that you understand the subject and its methods.
Build your argument in stages. In the minimum wage example, each separate point of analysis ends with a conclusion, and those conclusions build towards the overall judgement.
Keep your argument within the logic of economics: use terms such as “supply and demand” and follow the subject's usual style and structure.
Label diagrams and graphs clearly, acknowledge any made by others, and refer to each one directly in the body of your essay.
Use headings to organise your essay where they help.
pitfalls: Relying on content alone. Without economics concepts, methods and theories, your essay won't be grounded in economics.
A research question or research methods that don't clearly fit economics.
Reporting studies without evaluating them. In the minimum wage example, each counterargument is judged by the nature of its evidence and the studies carried out.
A one-sided discussion. A balanced discussion looks at different perspectives on your topic, and your evaluation should weigh up the strengths and limitations of your essay.
Using economics terms as labels only. The guide asks you to use key concepts in a meaningful way that explains something.
Diagrams or graphs that are unlabelled, unacknowledged, or never referred to in the body of your essay.
rules: Your essay must include secondary research (a literature review).
Your topic must be considered in terms of economics, even if the same topic could be approached through another individuals and societies subject.
think: What does the economic theory you're testing predict, in one sentence?
What evidence could test that prediction: published studies, data banks, news articles or your own primary research?
Can you limit your research question to one place and a clear time period, like town “X” since 2010?
Can you use each economics term in your essay to explain something, not just to name it?
How strong is the evidence in the studies that disagree with your theory?
Without the economic theory, would your question become a geography or global politics question?

subject: Global Politics
distinctive: Global politics is in the individuals and societies group, so your essay explores a question about human experience and behaviour. The guide's two global politics examples follow one pattern. First, a literature review sets out key political concepts, such as power, conflict or the right to privacy. Next comes analysis of one or more real cases. Last, an evaluation links the facts of each case with the theories.

In global politics, relevant academic secondary sources back up your argument. You may also add primary data collected with suitable methods, but you don't have to. Your content alone won't make your essay a global politics essay. Global politics concepts, methods and theories are what let you build a well-constructed argument.

Here is how a broad interest like sport becomes a global politics essay: you explore global discourses (the ways people talk and write) about women in sports, and how those discourses shape political decisions about gender rights. The guide also names migration and governance in a digital age as real-world issues for the group.

sources.primary: Primary data is optional in global politics. Academic secondary sources carry your argument, and you may add primary data collected with suitable methods. For example, the guide's Snapchat example analyses the app's own privacy policy and the personal data the app needs.
sources.secondary: Relevant academic secondary sources back up your argument, and every extended essay must include secondary research (a literature review). Both global politics examples in the guide open with a literature review of the key concepts.

methods: Literature review of key political concepts, such as power, conflict, terrorism, leadership, feminism in politics and soft power. Your literature review builds the framework for your analysis.
Comparing cases in two countries, as in the example comparing responses to terrorist attacks in New Zealand and France.
Analysing one case through the documents the case produces, as in the example analysing Snapchat's data requirements and privacy policy.
Discourse analysis: the guide's sport example explores global discourses about women in sports.
Other research strategies for all individuals and societies subjects: case studies, critical analysis of a theory or concept, and in-depth analysis of a primary source.
choosing_topic: Your topic can come from your own life, from a current debate, from a topic in one of your favourite subjects, or from a topic related to a favourite subject but not covered in it.

Big real-world issues, such as migration, governance in a digital age or the environmental and climate crisis, can work. Turn the issue into a focused question and explore it from a global politics point of view.

Your topic must be considered in terms of one individuals and societies subject. A broad interest such as sport could fit several subjects. The guide's global politics version explores discourses about women in sports and political decisions about gender rights.
Your approach decides your subject. The concepts, methods and theories of global politics are what ground your topic in global politics.
Both global politics research questions in the guide name the case inside the question: New Zealand and France in one, Snapchat in the European Union in the other.

examples.rq: To what extent is female leadership better at facing conflict? Responses to terrorist attacks in New Zealand and France.
examples.why: The essay opens with a literature review of the concepts of power, conflict, terrorism, leadership, feminism in politics and soft power. Next, the essay analyses terrorist attacks and the responses to them in New Zealand under Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern and in France under President Emmanuel Macron. An evaluation of both cases leads to a conclusion that links facts with theories.

examples.topic: Big data, apps and human rights
examples.rq: To what extent is the large amount of personal data collected by mobile apps a breach of the right to privacy? The case of Snapchat in the European Union (EU).
examples.why: The essay reviews the literature on big data, human rights, universalism, interdependence, indivisibility, the right to privacy and data protection. Next, the essay analyses the personal data needed to download and use Snapchat, and Snapchat's privacy policy. The facts are then linked with the key concepts to build an argument and a conclusion that answers the research question.

structure: The guide's global politics examples move in three stages: a literature review of key concepts, analysis of the case or cases, and an evaluation that links the facts with the theories.

Make sure your research question and research methods clearly fit global politics. The guide suggests reading the global politics subject guide to check that you understand the subject and its methods.
Keep your argument within the logic of global politics: use the subject's terms and follow its usual style and structure.

Label diagrams, images, graphs and maps clearly, with all required elements (such as a scale and a key or legend). Acknowledge any made by others, and refer to each one directly in the body of your essay.
Use headings to organise your essay where they help.
pitfalls: Relying on content alone. Without global politics concepts, methods and theories, your essay won't be grounded in global politics.
Keeping facts and theories apart. Both of the guide's examples end by linking the facts of the case to the concepts from the literature review.
A research question or research methods that don't clearly fit global politics.
A one-sided discussion. A balanced discussion looks at different perspectives on your topic, and your evaluation should weigh up the strengths and limitations of your essay.
Using key concepts without applying them. The guide says applying key concepts in your writing is essential.
Maps, diagrams or graphs that are unlabelled, missing a scale or key, unacknowledged, or never referred to in the body of your essay.
rules: Your essay must include secondary research (a literature review).
Your topic must be considered in terms of global politics, even if the same topic could be approached through another individuals and societies subject.
think: Which political concepts, such as power, conflict, human rights or soft power, will your literature review need to define?
Can you name your one or two real cases inside your research question?
If you compare two cases, are the two cases similar enough that a difference between them tells you something about your concept?
Can academic secondary sources carry your argument, or will you need to analyse a document, such as a policy, yourself?
How will your conclusion link the facts of your case to the theories in your literature review?
Whose views on your case would a balanced discussion need to include?
